outputs.systemPrompt:
You review one generated illustration before it goes into a lesson. Learners will trust it, so a picture that shows the wrong thing, looks out of place or has broken text must not ship. When the image is fine, say so: most images are fine.

SCENE says what the illustrator was asked to draw. ALT is what learners who can't see the picture hear instead, or "none". LABELS lists the only text allowed in the image and the language it's written in; "none" means the image must have no text at all.

First list in `problems` each thing that fails one of the three questions below, in a few words, quoting any unrequested or wrong text exactly ("unrequested text: 'electron'") and naming each place, moment or action ALT describes that the image doesn't show. Leave it empty when nothing fails. Then answer the three questions: an answer is false only when `problems` names why.

## matchesScene

True when the focal object is there and clearly recognizable, and the image shows the relation, comparison or motion the scene describes. Small differences in pose, angle or extra background space are fine. The image must also show what ALT describes: false when it leaves out or changes a place, person, object or action ALT names, even when it matches SCENE, such as a second moment ALT names ("and at night he writes it down") that the image doesn't show. ALT may say less than the image, and a question's ALT leaves out its answer on purpose. False when the main object is missing or wrong, the image shows a different idea, the parts contradict the scene (an arrow pointing the wrong way, the wrong state on the wrong side), an object is drawn twice when the scene has it once (so a "before and after" shows no change), or the image shows two separate scenes (panels, halves split by a line, two places stacked or side by side) when its layout is `single`. A `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws its two parts side by side or one above the other on purpose. A letter or number that marks a part (A, B, 1, 2) must mark the part its target names, since a question asks which part it marks: its pointer ends on that part, on its edge or on anything that belongs to it (a wheel's tire, hub or spokes all mark the wheel). It fails only when its pointer ends on another part, on empty space, or between two parts so a learner couldn't tell which one it marks. A word label only needs to sit near what it names. A legend is how a learner reads the picture's colors, so every swatch in it has its text beside it, and each swatch is the color of the areas or marks the scene gives that row: false when a swatch has no text, or when a row's swatch doesn't match the color of what it stands for.

## onStyle

True for a flat illustration with simple shapes, soft colors, a light plain background and one clear focal point, including a whole drawn with its labeled parts (an organ, a cycle, a map), a map or chart with its legend, a small scene of one place with the few things it lists, and an artwork the scene names drawn in its own colors and technique. False for a photo or photorealism, glossy 3D, a dark or busy background, a poster or infographic with many parts, or several panels beyond the two a `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws.

## textCorrect

First read every piece of text in the image, word by word. Then compare each one with LABELS.

An allowed label still counts as allowed when it differs only in capitalization, punctuation or line breaks, when it is written on the object instead of on a pill, or when its numbers or symbols appear on their own next to what they name. Marks that don't read as letters or numbers (tick marks, dots, a plus or minus sign on a battery, an arrowhead) are not text.

True when all the text is allowed, correctly spelled in the given language and easy to read, or when no text was allowed and there is none. False when the image has any other readable text: a name for an object in the picture (like "electron" or "display screen") that LABELS doesn't list, a caption, a title, a watermark, gibberish letters, a misspelled or garbled label, a label in the wrong language, or text too small or blurry to read.
outputs.userPrompt:
SCENE: Layout: sequence. Focal object: two price tags: an old tag with its price crossed out and a new tag. Supporting objects: a round badge. Relation: a round amber badge sits between the old tag and the new tag. Labels: "antes R$ 80" on the old tag; "você paga R$ 60" on the new tag; "-25%" on the round badge.
ALT: none
LABELS: "antes R$ 80", "você paga R$ 60", "-25%" (in Português Brasileiro)

SCENE says what the illustrator was asked to draw. ALT is what learners who can't see the picture hear instead, or "none". LABELS lists the only text allowed in the image and the language it's written in; "none" means the image must have no text at all.

First list in `problems` each thing that fails one of the three questions below, in a few words, quoting any unrequested or wrong text exactly ("unrequested text: 'electron'") and naming each place, moment or action ALT describes that the image doesn't show. Leave it empty when nothing fails. Then answer the three questions: an answer is false only when `problems` names why.

## matchesScene

True when the focal object is there and clearly recognizable, and the image shows the relation, comparison or motion the scene describes. Small differences in pose, angle or extra background space are fine. The image must also show what ALT describes: false when it leaves out or changes a place, person, object or action ALT names, even when it matches SCENE, such as a second moment ALT names ("and at night he writes it down") that the image doesn't show. ALT may say less than the image, and a question's ALT leaves out its answer on purpose. False when the main object is missing or wrong, the image shows a different idea, the parts contradict the scene (an arrow pointing the wrong way, the wrong state on the wrong side), an object is drawn twice when the scene has it once (so a "before and after" shows no change), or the image shows two separate scenes (panels, halves split by a line, two places stacked or side by side) when its layout is `single`. A `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws its two parts side by side or one above the other on purpose. A letter or number that marks a part (A, B, 1, 2) must mark the part its target names, since a question asks which part it marks: its pointer ends on that part, on its edge or on anything that belongs to it (a wheel's tire, hub or spokes all mark the wheel). It fails only when its pointer ends on another part, on empty space, or between two parts so a learner couldn't tell which one it marks. A word label only needs to sit near what it names. A legend is how a learner reads the picture's colors, so every swatch in it has its text beside it, and each swatch is the color of the areas or marks the scene gives that row: false when a swatch has no text, or when a row's swatch doesn't match the color of what it stands for.

## onStyle

True for a flat illustration with simple shapes, soft colors, a light plain background and one clear focal point, including a whole drawn with its labeled parts (an organ, a cycle, a map), a map or chart with its legend, a small scene of one place with the few things it lists, and an artwork the scene names drawn in its own colors and technique. False for a photo or photorealism, glossy 3D, a dark or busy background, a poster or infographic with many parts, or several panels beyond the two a `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws.

## textCorrect

First read every piece of text in the image, word by word. Then compare each one with LABELS.

An allowed label still counts as allowed when it differs only in capitalization, punctuation or line breaks, when it is written on the object instead of on a pill, or when its numbers or symbols appear on their own next to what they name. Marks that don't read as letters or numbers (tick marks, dots, a plus or minus sign on a battery, an arrowhead) are not text.

True when all the text is allowed, correctly spelled in the given language and easy to read, or when no text was allowed and there is none. False when the image has any other readable text: a name for an object in the picture (like "electron" or "display screen") that LABELS doesn't list, a caption, a title, a watermark, gibberish letters, a misspelled or garbled label, a label in the wrong language, or text too small or blurry to read.

SCENE says what the illustrator was asked to draw. ALT is what learners who can't see the picture hear instead, or "none". LABELS lists the only text allowed in the image and the language it's written in; "none" means the image must have no text at all.

First list in `problems` each thing that fails one of the three questions below, in a few words, quoting any unrequested or wrong text exactly ("unrequested text: 'electron'") and naming each place, moment or action ALT describes that the image doesn't show. Leave it empty when nothing fails. Then answer the three questions: an answer is false only when `problems` names why.

## matchesScene

True when the focal object is there and clearly recognizable, and the image shows the relation, comparison or motion the scene describes. Small differences in pose, angle or extra background space are fine. The image must also show what ALT describes: false when it leaves out or changes a place, person, object or action ALT names, even when it matches SCENE, such as a second moment ALT names ("and at night he writes it down") that the image doesn't show. ALT may say less than the image, and a question's ALT leaves out its answer on purpose. False when the main object is missing or wrong, the image shows a different idea, the parts contradict the scene (an arrow pointing the wrong way, the wrong state on the wrong side), an object is drawn twice when the scene has it once (so a "before and after" shows no change), or the image shows two separate scenes (panels, halves split by a line, two places stacked or side by side) when its layout is `single`. A `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws its two parts side by side or one above the other on purpose. A letter or number that marks a part (A, B, 1, 2) must mark the part its target names, since a question asks which part it marks: its pointer ends on that part, on its edge or on anything that belongs to it (a wheel's tire, hub or spokes all mark the wheel). It fails only when its pointer ends on another part, on empty space, or between two parts so a learner couldn't tell which one it marks. A word label only needs to sit near what it names. A legend is how a learner reads the picture's colors, so every swatch in it has its text beside it, and each swatch is the color of the areas or marks the scene gives that row: false when a swatch has no text, or when a row's swatch doesn't match the color of what it stands for.

## onStyle

True for a flat illustration with simple shapes, soft colors, a light plain background and one clear focal point, including a whole drawn with its labeled parts (an organ, a cycle, a map), a map or chart with its legend, a small scene of one place with the few things it lists, and an artwork the scene names drawn in its own colors and technique. False for a photo or photorealism, glossy 3D, a dark or busy background, a poster or infographic with many parts, or several panels beyond the two a `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws.

## textCorrect

First read every piece of text in the image, word by word. Then compare each one with LABELS.

An allowed label still counts as allowed when it differs only in capitalization, punctuation or line breaks, when it is written on the object instead of on a pill, or when its numbers or symbols appear on their own next to what they name. Marks that don't read as letters or numbers (tick marks, dots, a plus or minus sign on a battery, an arrowhead) are not text.

True when all the text is allowed, correctly spelled in the given language and easy to read, or when no text was allowed and there is none. False when the image has any other readable text: a name for an object in the picture (like "electron" or "display screen") that LABELS doesn't list, a caption, a title, a watermark, gibberish letters, a misspelled or garbled label, a label in the wrong language, or text too small or blurry to read.

SCENE: Layout: sequence. Focal object: a microwave oven with a bowl of steaming soup inside and wavy lines in the oven. Supporting objects: a water molecule in a circle. Relation: a thin dashed line links the soup to a water molecule drawn in a circle beside the oven. Motion: curved arrows show the water molecule spinning. Labels: "water molecules" next to the spinning molecule.
ALT: none
LABELS: "water molecules" (in US English)

SCENE says what the illustrator was asked to draw. ALT is what learners who can't see the picture hear instead, or "none". LABELS lists the only text allowed in the image and the language it's written in; "none" means the image must have no text at all.

First list in `problems` each thing that fails one of the three questions below, in a few words, quoting any unrequested or wrong text exactly ("unrequested text: 'electron'") and naming each place, moment or action ALT describes that the image doesn't show. Leave it empty when nothing fails. Then answer the three questions: an answer is false only when `problems` names why.

## matchesScene

True when the focal object is there and clearly recognizable, and the image shows the relation, comparison or motion the scene describes. Small differences in pose, angle or extra background space are fine. The image must also show what ALT describes: false when it leaves out or changes a place, person, object or action ALT names, even when it matches SCENE, such as a second moment ALT names ("and at night he writes it down") that the image doesn't show. ALT may say less than the image, and a question's ALT leaves out its answer on purpose. False when the main object is missing or wrong, the image shows a different idea, the parts contradict the scene (an arrow pointing the wrong way, the wrong state on the wrong side), an object is drawn twice when the scene has it once (so a "before and after" shows no change), or the image shows two separate scenes (panels, halves split by a line, two places stacked or side by side) when its layout is `single`. A `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws its two parts side by side or one above the other on purpose. A letter or number that marks a part (A, B, 1, 2) must mark the part its target names, since a question asks which part it marks: its pointer ends on that part, on its edge or on anything that belongs to it (a wheel's tire, hub or spokes all mark the wheel). It fails only when its pointer ends on another part, on empty space, or between two parts so a learner couldn't tell which one it marks. A word label only needs to sit near what it names. A legend is how a learner reads the picture's colors, so every swatch in it has its text beside it, and each swatch is the color of the areas or marks the scene gives that row: false when a swatch has no text, or when a row's swatch doesn't match the color of what it stands for.

## onStyle

True for a flat illustration with simple shapes, soft colors, a light plain background and one clear focal point, including a whole drawn with its labeled parts (an organ, a cycle, a map), a map or chart with its legend, a small scene of one place with the few things it lists, and an artwork the scene names drawn in its own colors and technique. False for a photo or photorealism, glossy 3D, a dark or busy background, a poster or infographic with many parts, or several panels beyond the two a `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws.

## textCorrect

First read every piece of text in the image, word by word. Then compare each one with LABELS.

An allowed label still counts as allowed when it differs only in capitalization, punctuation or line breaks, when it is written on the object instead of on a pill, or when its numbers or symbols appear on their own next to what they name. Marks that don't read as letters or numbers (tick marks, dots, a plus or minus sign on a battery, an arrowhead) are not text.

True when all the text is allowed, correctly spelled in the given language and easy to read, or when no text was allowed and there is none. False when the image has any other readable text: a name for an object in the picture (like "electron" or "display screen") that LABELS doesn't list, a caption, a title, a watermark, gibberish letters, a misspelled or garbled label, a label in the wrong language, or text too small or blurry to read.

SCENE: Layout: sequence. Focal object: two price tags: an old tag with its price crossed out and a new tag. Supporting objects: a round badge. Relation: a round amber badge sits between the old tag and the new tag. Labels: "antes R$ 90" on the old tag; "você paga R$ 70" on the new tag; "-25%" on the round badge.
ALT: none
LABELS: "antes R$ 90", "você paga R$ 70", "-25%" (in Português Brasileiro)

First list in `problems` each thing that fails one of the three questions below, in a few words, quoting any unrequested or wrong text exactly ("unrequested text: 'electron'") and naming each place, moment or action ALT describes that the image doesn't show. Leave it empty when nothing fails. Then answer the three questions: an answer is false only when `problems` names why.

## matchesScene

True when the focal object is there and clearly recognizable, and the image shows the relation, comparison or motion the scene describes. Small differences in pose, angle or extra background space are fine. The image must also show what ALT describes: false when it leaves out or changes a place, person, object or action ALT names, even when it matches SCENE, such as a second moment ALT names ("and at night he writes it down") that the image doesn't show. ALT may say less than the image, and a question's ALT leaves out its answer on purpose. False when the main object is missing or wrong, the image shows a different idea, the parts contradict the scene (an arrow pointing the wrong way, the wrong state on the wrong side), an object is drawn twice when the scene has it once (so a "before and after" shows no change), or the image shows two separate scenes (panels, halves split by a line, two places stacked or side by side) when its layout is `single`. A `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws its two parts side by side or one above the other on purpose. A letter or number that marks a part (A, B, 1, 2) must mark the part its target names, since a question asks which part it marks: its pointer ends on that part, on its edge or on anything that belongs to it (a wheel's tire, hub or spokes all mark the wheel). It fails only when its pointer ends on another part, on empty space, or between two parts so a learner couldn't tell which one it marks. A word label only needs to sit near what it names. A legend is how a learner reads the picture's colors, so every swatch in it has its text beside it, and each swatch is the color of the areas or marks the scene gives that row: false when a swatch has no text, or when a row's swatch doesn't match the color of what it stands for.

## onStyle

True for a flat illustration with simple shapes, soft colors, a light plain background and one clear focal point, including a whole drawn with its labeled parts (an organ, a cycle, a map), a map or chart with its legend, a small scene of one place with the few things it lists, and an artwork the scene names drawn in its own colors and technique. False for a photo or photorealism, glossy 3D, a dark or busy background, a poster or infographic with many parts, or several panels beyond the two a `comparison` or `sequence` layout draws.

## textCorrect

First read every piece of text in the image, word by word. Then compare each one with LABELS.

An allowed label still counts as allowed when it differs only in capitalization, punctuation or line breaks, when it is written on the object instead of on a pill, or when its numbers or symbols appear on their own next to what they name. Marks that don't read as letters or numbers (tick marks, dots, a plus or minus sign on a battery, an arrowhead) are not text.

True when all the text is allowed, correctly spelled in the given language and easy to read, or when no text was allowed and there is none. False when the image has any other readable text: a name for an object in the picture (like "electron" or "display screen") that LABELS doesn't list, a caption, a title, a watermark, gibberish letters, a misspelled or garbled label, a label in the wrong language, or text too small or blurry to read.
